Clark, Orhan Firat, Michael Auli, Sebastian Ruder, Jason Riesa, Melvin Johnson (Google Research, Hugging Face, Meta AI)
description: XTREME-S (Cross-lingual Transfer Evaluation of Multilingual Encoders for Speech) is a benchmark for evaluating universal cross-lingual speech representations. It covers 102 languages from 10+ language families, 3 different domains, and 4 task families: speech recognition, classification, speech-to-text translation, and retrieval. It includes datasets such as Fleurs, MLS, VoxPopuli, CoVoST-2, and Minds-14, and introduces a new massively multilingual evaluation dataset called Fleurs in all 102 languages.

name: XTREME-S
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: For Fleurs, between one and three speech recordings were collected per sentence (2.3 on average) in 102 languages. Speakers of the train sets are different from speakers in the dev/test sets to avoid speaker overfitting. The dataset uses 2009 n-way parallel sentences from the FLoRes dev and devtest sets as the text source.
rai:dataBiases: The benchmark acknowledges a significant performance gap between Western European languages and other language groups (e.g., Sub-Saharan African, South Asian), partly due to larger amounts of unlabeled data available for Western European languages in MLS and VoxPopuli. Reducing the gaps across geographical groups is identified as an important research direction. The benchmark covers 102 languages but notes that language coverage should not be unnecessarily large to avoid cumbersome evaluations.
rai:dataCollection: XTREME-S aggregates several existing multilingual speech datasets (MLS, VoxPopuli, CoVoST-2, Minds-14) and introduces a new dataset called Fleurs. Fleurs is the speech version of the FLoRes machine translation benchmark, using 2009 n-way parallel sentences from the FLoRes dev and devtest sets in 102 languages. Between one and three recordings were collected per sentence (2.3 on average), with new train-dev-test splits of 1509/150/350 sentences respectively. Training sets have around 10 hours of supervision. Speakers of the train sets are different from speakers in the dev/test sets.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The benchmark aggregates existing datasets: Multilingual LibriSpeech (MLS, derived from Librivox audiobooks), VoxPopuli (European Parliament sessions), CoVoST-2 (speech translation corpus), and Minds-14 (e-banking spoken intent data). The new Fleurs dataset is built from 2009 n-way parallel sentences from the FLoRes dev and devtest sets, recorded as speech in 102 languages.
rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Manual Human Curator
rai:dataLimitations: Results are much better on Western European languages than on other groups like Sub-Saharan African or South Asian languages, partly due to larger amounts of unlabeled data in Western European languages. The Fleurs dataset is complete at more than 97%, with some slight improvements and changes possible in a second version (e.g., missing recordings or replaced low-quality recordings). Tasks are focused on linguistic aspects of speech; nonlinguistic/paralinguistic aspects relevant to speech synthesis or voice conversion are not evaluated.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For Fleurs, new train-dev-test splits were built with 1509/150/350 sentences for train/dev/test respectively. For Minds-14, monolingual datasets were merged into a single multilingual dataset with a 30-20-50% train-dev-test split. For VoxPopuli, only the 14 languages with more than 10 hours of data from the ASR task were used. For MLS, the official 10-hour splits provided by the original authors were used. Scripts to download and reproduce preprocessing steps are provided.
rai:dataSocialImpact: XTREME-S aims to make speech technology available in all languages, giving speakers of under-represented languages an equal voice on the Internet and the possibility to make their content and culture known outside of their language cluster. The benchmark encourages data-efficient self-supervised representation learning to enable speech technology for low-resource languages.
rai:dataUseCases: Evaluating universal cross-lingual speech representations; benchmarking multilingual speech models on speech recognition (ASR), speech-to-text translation (ST), speech classification (language identification and intent classification), and speech retrieval tasks; catalyzing research in universal speech representation learning across 102 languages.

null_reasons.rai:annotationsPerItem: The paper mentions 1-3 recordings per sentence on average (2.3) for Fleurs, but this refers to speech recordings, not annotation labels per item in the traditional sense.
null_reasons.rai:annotatorDemographics: No demographic information about annotators/speakers is provided in the paper.
null_reasons.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: No inter-annotator agreement metrics or annotation quality analysis are discussed in the paper.
null_reasons.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: No specific annotation platform (e.g., MTurk, Label Studio) is mentioned in the paper.
null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: The paper notes Fleurs is complete at more than 97% but does not describe a protocol for handling missing data beyond noting some recordings may be missing or low-quality.
null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: No specific timeframe for data collection is mentioned in the paper.
null_reasons.rai:dataImputationProtocol: No imputation protocol is described in the paper.
null_reasons.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: No post-collection data manipulation protocol (augmentation, resampling, etc.) is described for the dataset itself.
null_reasons.rai:machineAnnotationTools: No machine annotation tools are described as part of the dataset creation pipeline.
null_reasons.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: No discussion of personal or sensitive information in the dataset is present in the paper.
null_reasons.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: No formal versioning or maintenance plan is described, though the paper mentions updates may be made on their platform for Fleurs.
